name: Virgin
lede: Virgin is a clear mid blue, entered in a 1930 color dictionary under a name that points to the Virgin Mary, whose blue robe is one of the most durable color conventions in Western art.

sections.title: A dictionary name
sections.body:
The swatch is a mid [[blue]] that sits between [[steel-blue]] and [[flat-blue]], about 3 color units from steel blue [9]. Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* of 1930 lists it as Virgin, on plate 35 K 7, and gives 1917 as the first recorded use of the name [9]. Our library files it among names from fashion and textiles [9].

Why the name was given is undocumented in the books we read. The Marian reading is natural, because Mary's robe is the best-known blue in art, but no source here connects the dictionary entry to it [9]. What can be told with sources is the history behind that reading, and it is surprisingly late and surprisingly costly.

sections.title: Mary before blue
sections.body:
Mary was not always dressed in blue. Pastoureau notes that images from before the twelfth century show her in a range of dark colors: black, grey, brown, violet, dark blue or dark green, chosen to convey grief for her crucified son [2]. That echoed the habit of wearing black or dark clothes to funerals [2].

Blue itself was a minor color in the early Middle Ages [1]. It served as a background to suggest majesty and divine presence, and now and then it dressed an emperor, the Virgin or a saint, but never as a bright hue; it was a dark shade close to grey or violet [1]. Around the year 1000, blues in manuscripts became clearer and lighter [1].

sections.title: The twelfth-century turn
sections.body:
From the twelfth century, Pastoureau argues, the cult of the Virgin made blue a prominent color in her images, and from there a color of sanctity [2]. Around 1140, the glass painters working for Abbot Suger at Saint-Denis perfected a famous blue [2]. The window of the Virgin at Chartres, usually known as Notre-Dame de la Belle Verrière, dates from the middle of the twelfth century and was reinstalled around 1215 to 1220 after a fire [2].

The Capetian kings of France bore a blue shield with gold lilies, and Pastoureau thinks blue was probably chosen as the royal color in homage to the Virgin, with Suger and Bernard of Clairvaux almost certainly involved [2]. He treats this as likely, not documented [2]. Blue then spread through heraldry, and Arthur's coat of arms became a blue field with three gold crowns between 1260 and 1280 [2].

Gothic art did not tie Mary to blue alone, though it remained her main color until the early modern period [2]. The Baroque brought a fashion for a gilded Virgin, which held on into the nineteenth century [2].

sections.title: Why the robe was blue: cost
sections.body:
Ball adds a material argument. Ultramarine, made from [[gem:lapis-lazuli|lapis lazuli]], was so expensive that using it conferred virtue on a sacred work, and the Virgin's ubiquitous blue robe shows this most clearly [4]. When artists began working by private contract, patrons often specified the pigment in order to show their own piety and wealth [4].

The contracts survive in some cases. In 1434 the painter Saladijn de Stoevere was told that his Virgin in an altarpiece for the Franciscan church in Ghent should wear a robe of gold cloth lined with *azure*, meaning ultramarine or [[gem:azurite|azurite]], and glazed with crimson lake [3]. In 1446 a contract for the church at Antoing named azurite [3]. Pacheco wrote almost a century after the Brueghel altarpiece that even wealthy Spanish painters could not obtain ultramarine, and Brueghel the Elder used cheap smalt for the Virgin's robe in his 1564 *Adoration of the Kings* [4].

Ball also corrects a popular idea. Itten held that the Virgin's blue in medieval art is mainly symbolic, but Ball says this overlooks the pigment itself [6]. Both explanations are true at once: the color was holy because it was the costliest [4][6].

Jarman, writing as a poet, repeats a Renaissance idea from Ficino that the Virgin's mantle is the [[sky-blue|sky]] [8].

sections.title: Pale blues, crimson, and what time did
sections.body:
Painters varied the blue. Raphael softened the ultramarine of the Virgin's robe in the *Madonna Alba* with lead white [3]. Bellini lightened his Virgin's blue only to a minimum, which left the folds shallow, while Titian made it much paler [4]. Titian paired a red gown with a blue robe in his Pesaro altarpiece [3]. Jan van Eyck robed the Virgin with Chancellor Rolin in crimson, whose purplish tint recalled the most valued dye of antiquity [7].

Time has changed some of these blues. Fourteenth- and fifteenth-century Madonnas were often robed in purplish ultramarine glazed with red lake, and in several the lake has faded, leaving the robe pale pink and deep bluish-purple in the shadows [5]. In *The Virgin and Child before a Firescreen* (about 1440) the robes are nearly as pale as paper, where Ball suggests they were probably a warm mauve [5]. Azurite can darken almost to black, as in the robes of Dieric Bouts and Gerard David [5]. The blue we see on a museum wall is not always the blue that was painted.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, the swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 35 works, or 0.15 per cent [10]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test [10].

It is mostly a modern color in the archive: 11 of 1,674 works from the 1900s, about 4.5 times the archive's rate, and 2 of 140 Impressionist works, almost ten times the rate [10]. Examples include Monet's [[painting:nga-46523|The Houses of Parliament, Sunset]], Jawlensky's [[painting:nga-130841|Still Life with Bottles and Fruit]] and Sargent's [[painting:commons-Q106357135|Atlantic Storm]] [10].

The earliest match is Fra Angelico's [[painting:commons-Q22082602|Madonna of the Pomegranate]] of 1426, where the color covers about 13 per cent of the canvas, 504 years before the name was first listed in our sources [10][9]. That is a look-alike in an aged photograph, not proof of what the painter used, but it is a fitting first [10]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid tone (51 per cent of the time), with shadow (31 per cent) and highlight (17 per cent) following [10]. Where to look: the robes in a medieval or early Renaissance Madonna, remembering that the red glaze may be gone and the azurite may have darkened [5].

questions.q: Why does the Virgin's blue robe appear so often in medieval and Renaissance art, according to Ball?
choices: Ultramarine was so costly that using it conferred virtue on the work
Blue was the cheapest pigment available
Church law forbade any other color for Mary
questions.answer: Ultramarine was so costly that using it conferred virtue on the work

questions.q: True or false: before the twelfth century Mary was usually shown in bright blue.
A pale, paper-white robe in a 1440 Madonna may once have been warmer because...

openers: Before the twelfth century Mary was usually shown in dark colors; blue became hers as the cult of the Virgin grew [2].
A 1434 contract told a Ghent painter to line the Virgin's gold robe with azure and glaze it with crimson lake [3].

issues: Dictionary name 'Virgin' origin undocumented; Marian link is a reading, not sourced
Royal blue as homage to the Virgin is Pastoureau's inference
Concordance for this slug is mostly the Virgin Mary in general; no source discusses the Maerz and Paul entry
